newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat asks Clinton to delay Mideast summit.
newsitem.headline: Arafat asks Clinton to delay Mideast summit.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat asked President Bill Clinton on Monday to delay an Israeli-PLO summit scheduled for Tuesday in Washington until differences over the agenda were settled, a PLO official said.
"Arafat at dawn asked Clinton to delay the meeting," the official told Reuters.

An all night meeting between senior Palestinians, Israelis, U.S. and U.N. officials failed to solve problems over what would be on the table in Washington, including Arafat's demand that Israel close a tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem.

The official said Arafat had not received a reply from Clinton who called the summit to end Israeli-Palestinian violence sparked by the opening of the tunnel. The clashes killed nearly 70 people and endangered nearly five-years of U.S. Middle East peacemaking.
Arafat went to Egypt on Monday to discuss the agenda with President Hosni Mubarak who has not yet responded to Clinton's invitation. Mubarak had wanted to host the summit in Cairo.
Arafat wants Egypt at the summit as a counterweight to the United States, Israel's main ally.
"The idea was to agree on most everything here before going to Washington, but no conclusions were reached," Marwan Kanafani, an Arafat aide, said.
"Presidents Arafat and Mubarak are doing everything possible to make the summit succeed, we appreciate Clinton's courage in calling for this summit during an election campaign," Kanafani said.
Clinton telephoned Arafat on Sunday to invite him to the talks but Arafat withheld his formal acceptance pending Mubarak's participation. U.S. officials said they expected Arafat to attend.

Kananfani called the meeting between PLO official Mahmoud Abbas, also known as Abu Mazen, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's political adviser Dore Gold, a failure. The U.S. ambassador to Israel, Martin Indyk, the U.S. Consul General in Jerusalem, Edward Abington, and U.N. coordinator Terje Larsen were also at the meeting, PLO sources said.

"The Israelis refused to agree on any political issues. They wanted to discuss security issues. They are not serious, and Arafat has no desire to meet Netanyahu just for the sake of meeting him," said a senior PLO official, who declined to be identified.

"Arafat wants to put an end to the reasons which led to this current crisis, to put a new basis for advancing the peace process, and this means being serious and sincere about commitment to the Oslo accords, and to implement signed agreements without any hesitation," the official said.

Arafat wants Netanyahu's new right-wing government to honour the Oslo self-rule accords signed by its predecessor and redeploy Israeli troops in the West Bank town of Hebron. Netanyahu wants to modify security arrangements for Jewish settlers in Hebron.
